stories.body:
Forums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say experts

Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.

Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.

In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”

Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.

Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.

The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.

Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.

Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.

“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”

Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.

“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.

In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.

Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.

Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

stories.title: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid: Drives like an EV, but there's no plug involved
stories.summary: Nissan’s series hybrid e-Power system has been retuned for American roads.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Nissan’s series hybrid e-Power system has been retuned for American roads.

Nissan has a new version of its bestselling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested in February. Most hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid.

That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V . Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars’ gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiasts irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for.

Series hybrids

Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher.

This charges a 1.67 kWh lithium-ion traction battery that has been optimized for its charge and discharge ability, which in turn powers a pair of electric motors. At the front axle sits a 202 hp (150 kW), 243 lb-ft (330 Nm) permanent synchronous magnet motor, at the rear another PSM providing 134 hp (100 kW) and 144 lb-ft (195 Nm), although given the battery’s limitations, combined power output is 225 hp (168 kW). And as you would expect, the motors will regeneratively brake under deceleration to return as much energy to the battery for reuse as possible.

Although this is the first time Nissan has offered the e-Power hybrid system in the US, it has been on sale in Japan for a decade now, with more than 1.4 million cars on the road in that time. Those versions weren’t considered quite sufficient for our roads, so Nissan retuned the system for the Rogue Hybrid to be able to cope with harder acceleration and bigger vehicles.

Enjoyable to drive

From behind the wheel, you could very easily forget this wasn’t just a new EV—a replacement for the gone-too-soon Ariya, perhaps. Throttle tip-in is immediate, like any good electric car, and there’s enough torque to get you on your way without any fuss, even if a 0–60 mph (97 km/h) time of 6.4 seconds isn’t particularly fast by 2026 standards. Nissan has had plenty of expertise in calibrating one-pedal driving setups, and when you access the Rogue Hybrid’s by pushing a button on the center console, you’ll find it’s no different here.

So keen was Nissan to demonstrate the smoothness with which the powertrain decelerates under regen braking that it put us through a mini school-run obstacle course, complete with a fishbowl full of water mounted to the cupholder. Nary a drop was spilled, versus the same test in what might be the Rogue Hybrid’s greatest rival, Toyota’s hybrid RAV4 . (The RAV4, with no one-pedal driving, requires you to use the brake pedal to slow and stop.)

Acceleration is good at highway speeds, and cruising is quiet—on a wet and windy day it was the gusts we heard, rather than wind noise generated by the car. Speaking of generators, you don’t really hear the engine running much either. It never revs particularly high and shuts off whenever possible—with music playing on the infotainment system, the occupants might not even notice.

The ride absorbed bumps well, but it didn’t absorb sharp transient shocks as well as it did those of longer duration. A combination of low-rolling resistance tires and Californian roads that were seeing their first rain in some time conspired to create rather a lot of understeer as I entered a roundabout with perhaps a touch more vigor than normal. That said, I rather liked the Rogue Hybrid’s steering feel, and together with the smooth power delivery from the two electric motors and the easy one-pedal driving mode, my time behind the wheel was most pleasant.

To live with?

The Rogue Hybrid SR we drove is rated at 41 mpg (5.7 L/100 km) in the city, 36 mpg (6.5 L/100 km) highway, and a combined 38 mpg (6.2 L/100 km), not quite as good as the RAV4 hybrid but still competitive with the segment.

The Rogue Hybrid provided a commendable amount of storage space, and I was glad to see so many physical controls. As our car was fitted with the Tech package, it included a larger 14.3-inch touchscreen infotainment system running Android Automotive OS with Google Automotive Services. Wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay are available with both this and the standard 12.3-inch system, and I was surprised to discover that the Rogue Hybrid would show Google Maps navigation from an iPhone through CarPlay on the main instrument display in front of the driver—usually only Apple Maps (and Waze iirc) appear on this screen, with Google Maps relegated to the infotainment display.

Seat comfort has long been a Nissan obsession, and its work on its “Zero Gravity” seats has paid off, as a day of driving did not result in a fatigued driver. The stitching and design of the seats were inspired by cozy puffer jackets, although I think the charcoal interior would be a better idea for life with a family or animals than the light gray of our test car.

Initially, Nissan will just have a single model of Rogue Hybrid for sale, the SR with the Tech Package, which will cost $41,490. In January, it will add the $35,490 SV and the $43,490 Platinum trims to the mix, prices that are benchmarked against the aforementioned Toyota. And for those who think you’ll only be able to find the most expensive ones at the dealership, Nissan says it expects the mix to be 30 percent SV, 50 percent SR, 20 percent Platinum.

Honest question: what is the ultimate benefit of these hybrids? They burn slightly less fossils, but can also burn the same or more, depending how they are driven. And have much higher complexity than a pure BEV or petrol.

stories.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
stories.summary: Shares in Intel continue to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 30 October 2026, 14:50 GMT

Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).

Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.

Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.

While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.

Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.

Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday, taking more than $500bn (£374bn) off its market value after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.

At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.

The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.

The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.

On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.

"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.

In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.

Amazon and Reddit down

Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.

The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.

Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading.

Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.

Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.

Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.

Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.

He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".

"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."

'Investors have turned ruthless'

Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.

The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.

Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.

"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.

"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."

However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.

While the Nasdaq closed 2.8% lower, it is up 7.8% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 8% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.3%.

Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.

"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

‘Even though economists warned that tariffs would be inflationary, Trump has enthusiastically embraced them’

Donald Trump successfully campaigned for his second term two years ago promising to reduce prices on day one , but ever since he returned to the White House, he has done little to fight inflation or reduce prices. Instead, some of his most important policy decisions – most notably his war against Iran and his tariff wars – have increased inflation instead of reducing it. This helps explain why more than one in five Americans who voted for Trump now disapprove of the job he’s doing.

Even though economists warned that tariffs would be inflationary, Trump has enthusiastically embraced them during his second term. Indeed, the “ liberation day ” tariffs he imposed soon after returning to office increased the price of hundreds of goods, including citrus fruits , steel, bananas, beef and auto parts. When the supreme court overturned those tariffs as illegal, Trump immediately imposed new 10% across-the-board tariffs that again helped push up prices (a lower court found those tariffs unlawful, too ). Time and again, Trump has slapped on new tariffs even though they inherently push up prices because tariffs are a tax on imported goods. Little wonder that a Fox News poll this month found that 77% of Americans disapprove of how Trump has handled tariffs.

Candidate Trump pledged to slash “energy and electricity prices by half” , to get “gasoline below $2 a gallon” , and to bring down “airfares and housing costs”. He has failed to do any of those things. Gas now averages $4.28 a gallon nationally, according to AAA . Yale Budget Lab says Trump’s tariffs will cost the average household $1,100 this year, while Moody’s Analytics says the war with Iran has already cost US households about $2,000 from higher energy, fuel and transportation costs and from higher interest rates.

Worsening Americans’ affordability problems, prices have been rising faster than workers’ wages in recent months. As a result, Americans have seen no real wage growth on average since Trump returned to office – both average hourly pay and prices have risen by 5.4% since January 2025.

Matthew Middleton, a White House spokesman, defended Trump’s record on inflation and critiqued Joe Biden’s, saying: “President Trump has implemented an aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda that has blunted Biden’s historic 40-year high inflation crisis, driven economic growth, increased wages and created private-sector jobs in areas that had been hollowed out and shipped overseas.”

After returning to the White House, Trump helped push up electricity prices by ending federal subsidies for low-cost renewable energy . His gung-ho cheerleading for datacenters, along with his speeding up of federal permitting to build them , has helped fuel a datacenter construction boom that is expected to increase electricity costs to consumers by more than $6bn . Trump and the Republican-led Congress further hit consumers by raising the cost of many electric vehicles by $7,500 when they ended EV subsidies.

When Trump plunged into war against Iran eight months ago, he showed little concern about what that war would mean for inflation back home. He ignored warnings that the war would cause Iran to close the strait of Hormuz , which in turn would cause oil and gas prices to soar. Since the war began, US gas prices have risen by over 40%, diesel prices by nearly 70%, and some fertilizer prices by 20% . Record diesel prices have pushed airfares skyward, while soaring diesel and fertilizer prices have created a sea of red ink for US farmers.

In one tiff over inflation, after Trump said last June “ I love the inflation ,” Senator Bernie Sanders responded , “You know who doesn’t love inflation, Mr President? Working families struggling to afford gas, groceries and other necessities because of your disastrous actions.”

Further defending Trump’s record on inflation, White House spokesman Middleton said: “The President has always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but this administration will continue to deliver economic wins for the American people over the next two years. While Democrats pretend to care about ‘affordability’, this administration has delivered tangible wins to make life more affordable for American families: President Trump signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals and will continue to put American workers first.”

A White House official added that Trump’s policies “have created an environment for sustained increase in energy supply and lower costs for American households and businesses”. Those policies have included making it easier to drill for oil and reducing business and environmental regulations.

Trump’s moves have further worsened Americans’ affordability woes by pushing up interest rates. By the time Biden left office, inflation, which had soared to a painful 9% during the pandemic, had slid to 3.0% and was heading lower. But Trump’s policies have played a major role in pushing inflation back up to 3.7% . That has caused the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, while also pushing mortgage rates higher. Thirty-year fixed mortgage rates have climbed to 7.4%, making it considerably harder for young and non-affluent Americans to buy homes. (As for Trump’s 2024 promise to reduce housing costs, he refused to sign a bipartisan bill that sought to speed housing construction with the aim of making housing more affordable.)

Under Trump, not only has the national debt climbed above $40tn, but this year’s federal budget deficit will reach $2tn. That worsening fiscal picture has worried bond investors and pushed up interest rates. (In 2019, Trump promised to eliminate the entire national debt within eight years.)

Trump’s policies have increased healthcare costs for millions of Americans. By pushing Congress to cut Medicaid by $1tn and to not extend Obamacare subsidies, Trump helped cause more than 20 million people to lose health coverage or pay more out-of-pocket for healthcare. Americans who pay for their own health insurance saw their premiums jump by 25% this year , with many households paying not just hundreds of dollars more, but thousands more.

To be sure, Trump has taken several steps to fight inflation, but most have been minor. His TrumpRX program has offered many drugs at lower prices, and that was one factor among many that contributed to the 4.5% drop in prescription drug prices over the past year. In August, Trump announced he would import 660m pounds of ground beef from Latin America to reduce beef prices – that move (which angered ranchers) was a direct response to the public outcry over the higher beef prices resulting from his tariffs. Last November, in a sharp about-face aimed at reducing prices, Trump rescinded his tariffs on coffee and tropical fruits after consumers had grown angry that coffee and citrus prices had soared due to Trump’s tariffs.

With his promise to pay $5,000 to every adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, Trump is essentially saying he will make it up to voters for pushing up prices and worsening affordability problems. Trump says the money for those payments could come from tariff revenues , but guess where those tariffs revenues come from? They come from the money that US consumers have had to pay on Trump’s tariffs – on his taxes on imports. Some might say that Trump wants to pay Peter by first robbing Peter.

Trump keeps saying that affordability problems are “a hoax” . But whenever average Americans go to a supermarket or gas station, they know that the affordability squeeze is real and a big issue in their lives. Many can see that Trump, despite his campaign promises, has done precious little to reduce inflation. Indeed, in very bad news for Republicans in the midterm elections, a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 78% of Americans blame Trump’s policies for pushing up prices.

stories.title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
stories.summary: The meeting involved representatives from the UK's four nations to discuss devolving more powers to regions and cities.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham met the first ministers from Scotland and Wales and representatives from Northern Ireland in Glasgow

Published 3 hours ago

The prime minister has said the UK's four nations must "move together" to devolve more power to regions and cities, following a meeting with the Scottish and Welsh first ministers in Glasgow.

Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind" after the sit-down, which also included representatives from Northern Ireland.

SNP leader John Swinney said he welcomed recognition that "Westminster is not working for Scotland" and pledged to work "constructively and collaboratively" with Burnham, while Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iowerth said the meeting was "positive".

Both first ministers have called for a wider conversation about independence but Burnham has ruled out referendums.

Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at PM Burnham Published 17 October

Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution' Published 16 October

First minister says Budget not serious about Wales ahead of meeting with PM Published 4 hours ago

Speaking after the first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow, Burnham highlighted plans for devolution at the regional level, saying he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind".

"It's really important we all move at the same pace together, and I won't allow anything to delay that," the prime minister said.

"Growth can't wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK."

Northern Ireland was represented by officials at the meeting amid the political fallout from the Drumcree parade dispute .

Burnham held talks with first ministers John Swinney (left) and Rhun ap Iowerth (right)

Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.

"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.

He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".

In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.

Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.

The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".

Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.

He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.

The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.

'Welcome start'

John Swinney said while he and Burnham disagree on independence, the meeting was "a welcome start" on further devolution.

"When the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will about," Scotland's first minister said.

"To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with the prime minister to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland - as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living."

A Downing Street spokesperson said the UK government would review issues raised by the first minister but this would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland.

Rhun ap Iowerth said: "I was pleased to meet with the prime minister in Glasgow today where I once again pressed the need for Wales and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools to better serve our communities.

"I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd."

He added he welcomed the prime minister's "step forward" on the Welsh government's fiscal and borrowing powers and gave his "full support" in pushing for a stronger relationship with the EU.

The prime minister had "positive discussions" with the Welsh leader, Downing Street said.

A spokesperson added: "The first minister of Wales agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

stories.title: Trump declares robot imports a national security threat
stories.summary: President orders trade talks on foreign-made factory robots, threatens tariffs.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
President orders trade talks on foreign-made factory robots, threatens tariffs.

President Donald Trump has declared the imports of foreign-made factory robots to be a national security threat—ordering new US negotiations with trading partners while holding out the possibility of imposing new tariffs on such robot imports in the future.

Issued on October 28, Trump’s presidential proclamation represents heightened government scrutiny of foreign-made industrial robots that could complicate the manufacturing operations of major US corporations that rely on such robots. Those companies include Detroit automakers General Motors and Ford, electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla , and aerospace and defense giants like Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Trump’s proclamation describes industrial robots and machinery as being crucial for producing US military weapon systems along with representing a “driving force” behind all critical infrastructure sectors within the US economy. The proclamation cites an investigation under US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick as having found that US imports of such robots “poses risks to the United States industrial base and threatens the long-term competitiveness of the United States in a sector that is increasingly vital to national security.”

The Department of Commerce investigation also supposedly found “unique security and safety risks” that may introduce “significant cybersecurity vulnerabilities that can result in severe consequences to the United States.”

Such wording echoes justifications used by Trump’s Federal Communications Commission when it banned new models of foreign-made robots, such as robotic vacuums, four-legged robot dogs, and humanoid robots, in July 2026. But that FCC action had specifically exempted industrial robot arms and other fixed or stationary robots commonly deployed in automotive factories and logistics warehouses.

Now Trump’s directive for the United States and trading partners “to adjust imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components” aims to strike new agreements on the issue within 180 days of the proclamation’s date. If no agreements have been reached by then, the proclamation warns that the president may take additional actions, like imposing “tariffs, duties, quotas, and fees” on such imports.

Any tariffs or other fees would, of course, be paid by the US companies importing such foreign-made robots. That would likely increase the cost of US manufacturing operations at a time when the United States has become the second largest market in using industrial robots, with the International Federation of Robotics reporting nearly 38,500 new US installations of industrial robots in 2025.

Major US automotive and aerospace companies often buy large robotic arms for factory floor work from the “big four” robotics makers—FANUC, ABB, Yaskawa, and KUKA—that are headquartered in Japan, Switzerland, and Germany. No US company currently offers comparable heavy-duty hardware for large industrial robotic arms, although the foreign robotics makers have been expanding their US engineering and assembly facilities.

Even Amazon, the company that has arguably deployed more robot workers than any other in the world, still uses some foreign-made robots, like Japan’s FANUC robotic arms, despite having significantly ramped up its own in-house robot production and developed certain specialized robotic arms.

Trump’s own proclamation acknowledges that US robotics companies do not produce enough industrial robots to “meet national security needs,” and that the United States “relies on foreign imports for most types of robotics and industrial machinery and for their components.”

If Trump eventually slaps tariffs on US imports of foreign-made industrial robots, that would at least fall short of restricting imports outright. Although as Intel recently showed, major US companies can still get waivers from the Trump administration to continue using foreign-made robots even when a nominal ban is in place.

stories.body:
The unprecedented number of empty seats at the fifth plenum – a symbol of expulsions – serve as a symbol for the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping

China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering , which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.

A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.

Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.

The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.

“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.

The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified , taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.

Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.

A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.

Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.

The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi, who is already the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong, is expected to secure a fourth term as party leader.

The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

stories.body:
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov (standing centre) is present at the G20 meeting in Atlanta, US

Published 30 October 2026, 17:08 GMT

European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in the US, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.

Two officials confirmed to the BBC the cancellation of the so-called family photo scheduled for Friday morning, which would usually include representatives from all the nations in attendance.

The meeting, which gathers top diplomats from the world's biggest economies, is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Ukraine is not not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.

Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is present and a diplomatic source confirmed the UK was among the countries which refused to participate in the picture.

One British official said: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".

A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".

"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.

In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.

The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of mid-term elections at the start of November, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".

Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.

Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

stories.title: Tech Tips for Parents this Digital Parenting Week
stories.summary: In today’s digital world, the internet is an essential resource for young people to access information, explore community, and find themselves. But we know that this often comes alongside fears of experiencing online harms like doxxing, grooming, or bullying. Trying to protect your family from everything all the time is impractical and exhausting, but some thoughtful planning can help families devise a workable plan that meets their needs and addresses their concerns. That’s why this Digital Parent Week, we’re sharing easy tips on how parents and their children can work together to co-curate a digital safety plan that helps all members of the family enjoy the benefits of technology while protecting their online privacy and safety. Start with Open Conversations Online safety begins with communication, not just restrictions. Talk with a young person about how they use the internet: their favourite apps, games, and social media platforms for example. Creating a supportive environment helps young people feel comfortable asking for help if something goes wrong online. Together, you can think about: What do we want to protect? e.g., I want to protect a young person’s privacy and mental health when they’re playing Roblox. How bad are the consequences if we fail? e.g, losing some money on a scam or having creepy conversations with strangers that could escalate into something more nefarious or dangerous. stories.title: Victory! You Can Now Exclude Apps from Siri AI
stories.summary: In the most recent update to Apple’s devices, iOS 27.2, the company has introduced a new setting to “Exclude Apps” from Siri AI, fulfilling one of our asks from our Encrypt It Already campaign earlier this year . One of our main concerns with new AI features on devices is how those features interact with end-to-end encrypted content, particularly with secure messaging apps. Many AI features require cloud processing, and despite privacy protections engineered into these systems , the content of secure messaging apps may leave a user’s device without their knowledge. That changes the privacy concerns around using those tools. In a perfect world, users would be able to put a barrier up to ensure data from certain apps doesn’t leave the device. Here was our initial ask: You should be able to tell the operating system’s AI to not access an app, even if that comes at the “cost” of missing out on some features. The setting should be straightforward and easy to understand in ways the Gemini and Apple Intelligence controls currently are not. At launch, we found the settings to control Siri AI’s app access behavior pretty confusing . You had to toggle several options to block Siri AI off from accessing an app, or disable Siri AI entirely. Turning off Siri AI and reverting to Siri Classic is, for now, still a good option if you’d prefer to use the older version. The most recent update is far more clear and does more to protect your data. And, just as expected, it comes at the cost of some features. That’s a good thing, actually. The features not working shows that the new setting is effective. Here’s how to add apps to the exclusion list, once you’ve updated to 27.2: Open Settings > Siri > Excluded Apps Tap “Add Apps” and select any apps you’d like to add to the exclusion list Now Siri AI cannot access the contents of the app. Excluding an app also means you may lose some features. For example, if you exclude the Apple Messages app, you will no longer be able to have Siri AI read or respond to messages for you. Even the “onscreen awareness” feature, where you invoke Siri and ask it for information about what you’re currently looking at, will not work anymore. For example, if you exclude Signal, you cannot invoke Siri and ask it to discern any information in the Signal app. You’ll just get these messages: What’s the State of This on Android? stories.title: Ghost in the machine: how AI is haunting the search for the supernatural
stories.summary: Ghost hunting has changed in recent years due to AI chatbots, and paranormal enthusiasts are concerned Ghost hunting is a tech-heavy pursuit. When Amy Waine and Jarrad Cutting investigate haunted locations, they’re loaded up with software of their own design, such as an app that assigns signals from a phone’s sensors to different words in a database. In the age of ChatGPT, the ghost-hunting pair is probing the world of AI. They describe one of their latest inventions, an app called GhostTube Seer , as “the world’s first AI Ghost Hunting tool”. In the hands of paranormal investigators, scientific tools like EMF meters (used to detect electromagnetic fields) are repurposed to identify changes and anomalies that they believe indicate supernatural activity. Seer is, in many ways, simply an expansion of that practice, another way to scan an empty room and believe that something may be there. The app, which requires a paid monthly subscription, has more than 1m downloads, according to its Google Play store listing . But for others in the ghost hunting world, AI is an unwelcome presence. Since the release of ChatGPT in 2022, AI-generated ghost stories and images of the supernatural have flooded online spaces, so much so that popular forums like the r/Nosleep subreddit , meant for scary stories, have implemented a strict policy against AI-generated material. stories.summary: Liquid Static Studio; PC You take on the role of flight attendant in this clever and absorbing retro-style game that veers from daft horror spoof to genuinely disturbing There was always something creepy about the job-simulator genre. All those mindless automatons queueing up to use your bus, bar or bed store, or whatever workplace you are trapped in for the duration of the game. The endless repetitive tasks. The emptiness of the world beyond your corporate existence. Together, these elements scream existential terror … which is perhaps why we are now seeing a new indie sub-genre of job sim horror games, including Home Safety Hotline, Dredge and more recently, Grease Trap ’99, a Lovecraftian mystery set in a Scottish chip shop. Now, we have Night Plane, in which you take on the role of a flight attendant on a jumbo jet to hell. It all starts kind of normally. You turn up for the first day of your new job, meet your colleagues, then take your spot at the departure gate, checking in customers and being careful to root out anyone with invalid tickets. Once on the plane, you roll your trolley down the aisle, serving booze and inedible meals, and occasionally dealing with passenger complaints. Wall Street closes sharply lower as AI cash burn fears spark tech selloff

All three ⁠major US stock indexes slumped on Friday, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq suffering the steepest loss.

The tech rout was sparked by disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon released late ⁠on Thursday.

Chip stocks veered sharply lower, dragging the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index to a monthly loss.

All three main equity indexes closed lower on the ‌week. The S+P 500 and the Nasdaq logged monthly losses, while the Dow exited October with a gain.

According to preliminary data, the S+P 500 lost 139.30 points, or 1.80%, ​to end at 7,580.21 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 747.73 points, or 2.84%, to 25,440.68. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 571.98 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.58.

Third-quarter earnings season has passed the halfway mark, with 299 companies in the S+P 500 having reported. Of those, 82% have beaten consensus expectations, according to LSEG ⁠data.

Analysts now expect third-quarter S+P 500 earnings growth of 31.6%, year-on-year, per LSEG.

Oil supermajors ​Exxon Mobil and Chevron ​both beat quarterly profit expectations, benefiting from ​soaring profit margins as a result of energy supply disruptions arising from the US-Israeli war ​with Iran and Russia’s ‌war in Ukraine.

Starbucks ​dipped after the ​coffee chain forecast an annual revenue decline due to its divestiture of its Chinese business.

Cryptocurrency-related firms Coinbase, Strategy, and Robinhood fell in the wake of reports that hackers stole $6.3bn from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Closing summary

US stocks tumbled on Friday, with ⁠the Nasdaq suffering its ⁠largest one-day ​percentage drop since 5 June . It followed disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon, which amplified growing worries surrounding AI-related companies’ massive spending on the nascent technology. Cryptocurrency-related firms Coinbase, Strategy , and Robinhood fell in the wake of reports that hackers stole $6.3bn from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

All three ⁠major US stock indexes slumped, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq suffering the steepest loss. According to preliminary data, the S+P 500 lost 139.30 points, or 1.80%, ​to end at 7,580.21 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 747.73 points, or 2.84%, to 25,440.68. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 571.98 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.58.

Experts identified North Korea as the likely culprit behind the biggest heist in history , and have said the hack was probably carried out by TraderTraitor , an elite north Korean hacking unit. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking, which is estimated to generate half of the country’s foreign currency income, generating revenues for its military , including its nuclear weapons programme.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers , which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been “additional points of breach” in a sophisticated attack. Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets.

The FBI said it is “aware of the incident and ‌is engaged with relevant public and private partners to ​understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate ⁠investigative steps”. The UK’s financial watchdogs are also monitoring for any potential fallout from the heist.

Cryptocurrency-related firms Coinbase, Strategy, and Robinhood fell in the wake of reports that hackers stole $6.3bn from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance has no ⁠cyber ​insurance and will fund customer reimbursements through company reserves after hackers stole $6.3bn in the world’s largest cryptocurrency heist, Reuters is reporting, citing a ⁠source close to the exchange.

Binance has said the attack began with a compromised employee laptop and involved multiple breach points. ⁠It found no evidence of private-key leakage and said roughly $3bn of affected assets ​had been frozen.

The exchange holds ‌directors’ and officers’ (D+O) liability insurance, ‌Reuters’s source said, describing crypto cyber insurance as “virtually impossible” for crypto ‌companies to obtain.

The source also said Binance’s Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) had no external insurance or reinsurance backing.

D+O cover could respond to claims against executives alleging failings in their oversight, rather than replace stolen assets.

Analysis: How crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programme

Defence and security editor

North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.

Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor , an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group . Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.

North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.

Kim Jong-un , its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine . But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.

A UN panel of experts , reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing “58 suspected cyber-attacks” by North Korea “on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023” worth $3bn.

The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.

The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world’s largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange – the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.

Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match . He said:

double quotation mark Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one.

The irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.

Read Dan’s full analysis here:

The $6.3bn Binance hack could mark an “inflection point” for digital ⁠asset insurance buying, with firms needing to look beyond large specie limits and examine the breadth of their ⁠protection, Relm CEO ⁠Joseph Ziolkowski told Reuters.

Exchanges ​and custodians had historically prioritised relatively inexpensive specie cover, he said, describing an approach of “form over function”. ⁠More than $1bn of specie limits was available globally, with less available for cyber cover including digital asset theft.

Ziolkowski described ⁠specie as largely protecting private keys. But a malicious intrusion elsewhere in ​a transaction approval process could ‌enable theft while those ‌keys remained intact.

Binance has said it found no evidence of private-key ‌leakage and identified multiple breach points.

Cyber policies could respond to such intrusions where their wording expressly included digital asset theft, Ziolkowski said. He argued buyers should examine protection across their operations and transaction signing arrangements.

Even holding cyber insurance would not ‌establish that a particular loss was covered, Ed Lewis, global lead for cyber and technology risks at RPC, told the news agency.

“A cyberattack ​tells you how the trouble started. It does not tell you which policy pays for the missing money,” he said.

A precautionary suspension of withdrawals might not satisfy the policy trigger for business interruption cover, ⁠Lewis said. Stolen assets, response costs, lost income and customer claims each ​required analysis ​against the facts and wording.

Binance ​has pledged to meet customer losses through its ​SAFU reserve and company ‌resources, announcing more ​than $6.34bn of ​company funds separate from roughly $3bn of frozen assets.

Lewis said frozen assets had not necessarily been returned, while customer reimbursement did not establish that an insurer was paying. “A record theft does not automatically become a record insurance loss,” ‌he said.

Tech stocks sell-off deepens, dragging Wall Street toward worst day since June

A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high, the Associated Press reported.

The S+P 500 dropped 1.9% and was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the month. The Nasdaq composite was likewise heading toward its worst day since June, as the weakness for technology stocks dragged it down 3.1%, as of 1:20 pm ET. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 511 points, or 1%.

The U.S. stock market remains only 3.1% below its record, which has boosted the value of workers’ 401(k) accounts, but the shakiness for stocks in the AI industry is coming just days before Tuesday’s upcoming US elections. Worries about AI in general have already become a general and bipartisan concern for voters, and Donald Trump has historically used the stock market’s performance as a measure of his own personal success.

In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack of Binance, the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a US-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6 billion worth of crypto at Binance.

Explainer: How big a deal is the $6.3bn Binance heist?

By Dan Milmo and Kalyeena Makortoff

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a $6.3bn heist that, according to experts, is likely to be the work of North Korea .

This is not the first time a crypto market has been targeted by hackers, and the rogue state has a track record of this type of theft. Here we answer some key questions about what’s happened:

Just how big a deal is this?

It could be the biggest heist of any kind in history, according to Elliptic, a consultancy specialising in crypto-related crime. The incident, which took place late on Thursday, is more than four times bigger than the previous largest crypto hack, the $1.5bn one targeting the Bybit exchange last year . Elliptic says there does not appear to be anything comparable in the pre-crypto era.

How was Binance hacked?

It does not appear that private keys were hacked. Instead, a Binance engineer’s laptop was infiltrated, which in turn allowed the attackers to drain “hot” wallets. Binance later added that there were “additional points of breach” in its systems as well as the laptop.

Do we know who did it?

This attack has been attributed to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor, a name assigned to it by the US government. The communist state, short of cash and hamstrung by sanctions, has a strong track record of crypto hacking. TraderTraitor emerged from Lazarus, a group working from North Korea’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, a military intelligence agency.

Read more questions answered here:

Stocks have tumbled following the hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange.

The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a US-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6bn worth of crypto at Binance.

Coinbase Global fell 12.7% even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4% of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 6%, AP reported.

It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons.

In the US , Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) chairman Michael Selig told reporters that “we have the ability to trace all this in the blockchain”.

Speaking to CNBC, Selig said it was “very concerning” that there had been “several cyber incidents involving crypto” and the CFTC has regulations in place to prevent this sort of attack.

He added that he wants to see a “federal option” so that people will register with the CFTC.

Summary: the day so far

Hackers have stolen $6.3bn from Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in what could be the largest theft ever.

The attack saw more than $6bn of crypto assets taken from Binance’s own ‘hot wallet’, apparently after a laptop belonging to one of Binance’s development and operations engineers was compromised.

Binance has committed to cover losses from its company funds, and says it is working with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.

double quotation mark “aware of the incident and ‌is engaged with relevant public and private partners to ​understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate ⁠investigative steps”.

The UK’s financial watchdogs are also monitoring for any potential fallout from the Binance heist.

Co-CEO Richard Teng has said this afternoon that ⁠the attacker used a self-destruct mechanism ⁠that destroyed ⁠tooling ​and traces as they went.

Teng also said Binance was conducting a full security review , and pledged:

double quotation mark “We will do everything in our power to make sure that these bad actors are held accountable.”

Security experts said the hack was probably carried out by TraderTraitor , an elite north Korean hacking unit .

Chainalysis said the hackers appeared to be using “never-seen-before laundering patterns” to avoid the stolen funds being frozen, by switching stablecoins into non-freezable assets such as ethereum.

stories.summary: When you think of the serial killer and former forensic psychiatrist Hannibal Lecter, what comes to mind? I would bet good money it’s Anthony Hopkins in Jonathan Demme’s 1991 film Silence of the Lambs, talking about eating someone’s liver with fava beans and a nice chianti. This film, an adaptation of Robert Harris’s book of the same name, projected the character into the cultural zeitgeist. There have been multiple adaptations of Harris’s four novels about Lecter since the first, Red Dragon , was released in 1981. These include Manhunter (1989), the Hannibal film (2001), Red Dragon (2002), the NBC series Hannibal (2013 to 2015), and more recently, a television series Clarice (2021), focusing on the events of The Silence of the Lambs. stories.body:
When you think of the serial killer and former forensic psychiatrist Hannibal Lecter, what comes to mind?

I would bet good money it’s Anthony Hopkins in Jonathan Demme’s 1991 film Silence of the Lambs, talking about eating someone’s liver with fava beans and a nice chianti. This film, an adaptation of Robert Harris’s book of the same name, projected the character into the cultural zeitgeist.

There have been multiple adaptations of Harris’s four novels about Lecter since the first, Red Dragon , was released in 1981. These include Manhunter (1989), the Hannibal film (2001), Red Dragon (2002), the NBC series Hannibal (2013 to 2015), and more recently, a television series Clarice (2021), focusing on the events of The Silence of the Lambs.

Lecter now makes his stage debut in an adaptation of The Silence of the Lambs.

Much like the film, this adaptation sees FBI trainee Clarice Starling sent to interview cannibal sociopath Dr Hannibal Lecter at the behest of her mentor, Jack Crawford. Crawford hopes that Lecter can shed some light on a recent spate of serial killings where women are being flayed by Buffalo Bill (real name Jame Gumb) to make a skin suit. In the conversations between Lecter and Clarice, an uneasy connection emerges. Clarice must find Bill’s latest victim, Catherine Martin, before time runs out.

Before going to see this adaptation, I wondered whether there would be any imitation of the visual elements of the film. Specifically, would there be a repetition of characteristics that came to define the character of Hannibal specifically?

There are moments of this throughout: the look of the cell and the mask, the slicked back hair and demeanour of Hannibal (played here by John Partridge), the night-vision goggles of the showdown between Buffalo Bill (Sam Jackson) and Clarice (Mollie Gallagher). This is perhaps necessary. Adaptations often bring with them what literary critic Linda Hutcheon calls “knowing audiences” who are familiar with the text and therefore may look for and want similarities.

Moving from the mediums the story has previously inhabited (novel, film, television) to stage offers the opportunity for new ways to tell this story, which the production takes advantage of.

The staging is impressive, neatly segueing between the asylum where Lecter is kept, the FBI training school Quantico, Jack Crawford’s (Oliver Farnworth) office and Buffalo Bill’s house where he holds women captive before killing them. The production’s switching between these settings feels smooth and characters inhabit mixed worlds in the storytelling. One notable sequence saw Buffalo Bill sitting atop Lecter’s cage sewing his skin suit while Clarice and Lecter discussed him. In this, Bill is physically and metaphorically hovering over them.

The production also employs interesting techniques to give the audience information in unique ways. These included the projection of the case files of a patient being discussed across the dark of the stage. Another is the screening of a press conference by Catherine Martin’s (Lottie Amor) mother (Jo Mousley) projected onto a fine screen across the stage, which becomes more transparent, allowing the audience to see events on the stage as she speaks. This multiplicity of action capitalises on the opportunities of theatre, and avoids any moment or storyline feeling too static.

One notable, and welcome, change is the characterisation of Buffalo Bill. In Demme’s 1991 film, the portrayal was seen as queerphobic and transphobic, leading to protests from activist groups .

As one leader of the LGBTQ+ media rights group Glaad commented at the time: “He has a poodle named Precious, he sews, he wears a nipple ring, he has an affected feminine voice, and he cross-dresses. He completely promotes homophobia.” (In more recent years, the portrayal has been recast as transphobia.)

The 1994 film Philadelphia, about the mistreatment of a gay man dying of Aids, is often viewed as a form of apology to the LGBTQ+ community for Silence.

This new theatre production, however, steps back from the controversy of the film. Instead, Bill is presented as childlike, often sitting cross-legged like at school, or roaming around the stage in his underwear (representing, in part, his “unfinished” nature).

John Partridge clearly relishes playing Hannibal Lecter, pacing around the stage in a catlike way. Aside from a few vocal echoes of Hopkins in his delivery – for instance, in the way he says “F…B…I” and “Quid pro quo, Clarice” – Partridge manages to offer a take on the character that avoids mimicry. His portrayal changes the physicality of Lecter, adds more energy than the template that Hopkins provided.

Similarly, Mollie Gallagher’s Clarice retains echoes of Foster in her voice, with the husky tones and approach to the accent strikingly similar. Maybe this is because Hopkins’s Hannibal mocks the background and West Virginian (Appalachian) accent in the film, imitating it while asking: “What is your father, dear? Is he a coal miner?”

The characters’ relationship is also altered on stage by their physical proximity to one another, developing more of a closeness and tension, which is absent in other adaptations.

The production overall gives some moments that re-address some of the concerns of previous adaptations. For instance, Buffalo Bill’s victim Catherine Martin. It delivers elements of familiarity for audiences, while allowing for subtle tweaks that reframe Harris’ text.

There are some commendable decisions here in adapting the screen to the stage. However, is it the most novel and inventive adaptation? Possibly not. But as a fan of Hannibal Lecter it was fun to see how this story could come alive in the theatre and I’m sure other fans will enjoy it too. For those who are new to the story, it still presents an engaging piece of theatre well worth seeing.

The Silence of the Lambs is running on a major UK and Ireland tour from October 2026 through to June 2027

stories.body:
John Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget was a picture of a government doing its best to offer “what help we can afford”, while weathering the economic storms. But despite its 98 policy measures, decisions on some of the biggest issues appear to have been kicked down the road.

In the meantime, it seems that the real incomes of UK households could fall by 1% next year. This forecast, from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), offered a grim picture. It also predicted UK economic growth of just 1% , as well as higher inflation and interest rates. The OBR, the government’s independent spending watchdog, has also suggested that by 2029-30 households will still be only 1% better off than they were ten years previously. This would be the slowest growth in real disposable household income for generations.

And in further bad news for households, the OBR estimated that the tax collected by the government as a percentage of GDP would reach record levels by 2030-31 – six percentage points higher than pre-pandemic levels. Taxes are already higher than at any time since the second world war.

The budget was enthusiastically backed by Labour members. But it can also be seen as a holding operation by the chancellor, reassuring the markets while leaving the prime minister the space to develop his vision of the causes close to his heart. These of course include social care, devolution and welfare reform. Notably, the only measure which in relative terms was generously funded was the £500 million allocated to end rough sleeping, the cause Burnham cited as his priority on his first day in office.

The limited measures to help with the cost of living reflect Burnham’s concerns about tackling the issue that most worries the public , but they are modest in scale and for the most part temporary.

Read more: Budget 2026: experts on what John Healey’s ‘breathing space’ plan means for households

The Treasury’s modest ambitions are reflected in the limited scale of the additional taxes it has announced to fund cost-of-living measures, especially to help with energy prices. The government has found some taxes it can raise and some efficiency savings it could make.

However, most of the cost-of-living measures – which will cost £6.5 billion this year – are only temporary, while some of the tax increases occur later in the parliament. As a result, the government expects that within five years the situation will be reversed, with Treasury revenues up by £7 billion .

One move that could have a long-term impact is Healey’s changes to the spending rules to protect “preventive spending” from department cuts. These are measures that have an initial cost but eventually save money. An example is the SureStart childcare programme , for example, which has been shown to improve long-term education prospects and reduce crime in deprived communities.

Back to welfare and defence

But the government has postponed its most difficult decisions – on defence, social care, devolution and welfare spending. The latter, the most politically challenging, awaits the publication of two key reports on welfare next month. The Timms and Milburn reviews will report respectively on personal independence payments, and the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

Any big decisions are likely to take shape after the publication of the prime minister’s ten-year plan (expected in December), and next year’s spending review, which will flesh out spending plans up to the next general election.

The urgent need to boost defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030 was the issue that led Healey to resign from the previous government. In his first budget as chancellor, despite insisting this target would be met, he was cagey on how it might be financed.

He cited “innovative financing measures”, which might include off-the-books contributions from the private sector through PFI (private finance initiatives) and the use of government investment banks, which may not be subject to the same fiscal rules. Healey also sees defence spending as part of the government’s industrial strategy, and ministers have announced that foreign firms that win defence contracts of more than £50 million will have to deliver benefits of the same amount back into the UK.

Another thing we do know is that defence investment will also be funded by forcing all other departments to cut their own spending by 1% . This is a pattern Healey may repeat to fund other new spending commitments.

In fact, the OBR estimates that, after taking into account the future spending plans of the “protected” departments (health, education and defence), all other departments would need to cut their own spending by 2.6% to allow the government to meet its 2030-31 fiscal target. This would mean less for roads, prisons, the police, housing, and higher education. “Efficiency savings” would be unlikely to close the gap.

The chancellor has taken over at a particularly difficult time for the world economy, and European nations are among the hardest hit. Healey will need luck as well as skill to navigate the shoals of a global slowdown. However, it is already clear that the prime minister’s desire for closer ties with Europe to boost growth is not shared by the chancellor.

Many events – from a resumption of full-scale warfare in the Strait of Hormuz to the possible collapse of the AI bubble – are beyond Healey’s control. He has temporarily reassured the bond markets with his cautious “do no harm” budget. But delivering improved living standards and better public services to a still-jaundiced electorate remains an enduring challenge.
