stories.body:
Artificial intelligence is already a transformative chapter in the story of mathematics, but it won’t be the final one.

Atoosa Kasirzadeh is a philosopher and mathematician. She is a research scientist at DeepMind Institute and an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University. Her research is focused on the social and scientific implications of AI.

In the past few months, unreleased frontier AI systems have significantly disrupted a classic conception of mathematics. They successfully established a complete formalization of Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, found a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem and — just a few days ago — generated hundreds of manuscripts that each purport to prove an important mathematical problem. Most recently, on October 26, another of the Clay Millennium Prize problems was felled by an AI system.

Mathematicians reacted with a volatile mixture of optimism, anxiety and deep disorientation. In July, for example, Kirwin Hampshire, a Ph.D. student in mathematics, published an essay he titled “The Dark Night of Mathematics” in which he voiced the fear that human mathematicians might soon become obsolete next to AI systems with far greater speed and memory. “I am suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to these developments,” he wrote. “I have been screaming internally for days. It feels as though I am living inside of a nightmare.” For Hampshire, the very act of doing mathematics — the human struggle, the human aesthetic judgment, the human feeling and value of finding, understanding and sharing a new proof — could become a quaint artisanal craft, with human mathematicians no longer needed to push the frontier of mathematics.

Some mathematicians have realized that they must radically rethink their professional role and identity in light of this new technological reality. I was recently at an AI conference where a Fields Medal winner gave a talk on the frontier capabilities of AI systems for math problems. They closed their talk by saying: “We need to develop new theories of care and love.” This call was quite telling: a world-class mathematical theorist asking for theories of a very different kind. The mathematician, it seems, might become a philosopher of care and love. In a short essay, Logan Graves, a mathematical philosopher, went further , suggesting that “the era of human mathematicians is ending, if not ended ”; human mathematicians should find a new purpose in life, he wrote, and “the future of the human mathematical community, and eventually all scientific communities, is the practice of priests, then that of monks. Not researchers.”

Terence Tao, a prominent Fields Medal winner and mathematics professor, acknowledged the deep complexity of this historical moment. Adopting a cautiously optimistic stance, he forecast that the mathematical “community will emerge stronger and more resilient than before.” Daniel Litt, a professor of mathematics at the University of Toronto, offered a set of core problems that should be solved for building the future of mathematics in an intriguing essay called “The End of Mathematics.” Litt wrote: “I’m broadly optimistic that mathematics will survive and flourish,” but that requires the mathematical community to address complex (not merely formal) questions such as redesigning institutions that incentivize high-quality scientific research and reorienting human capital.

Each of these reactions is entirely understandable; each represents a deeply respectable and admirable attempt to face and process a disruption to established ways of doing, being or becoming — of doing a certain type of mathematics and of being or becoming a particular type of mathematician.

Because these reactions respond to different dimensions of a complex concern, it is helpful to distinguish between four central questions that urgently need answers. First: What is mathematical progress, and how is mathematics actually advanced? Second: How is the epistemic and creative agency of practicing mathematicians being disrupted? Third: How should we educate future human mathematicians and sustain human mathematical capacities? And fourth: How should incentives, research and structures for reward and credit be reorganized?

I start by distinguishing between two models of mathematical progress. I call them the checklist model and the generative encounter model . In the checklist model, mathematical progress is primarily about incremental advancement in proving what humans, at a rather recent point in our history, have designated a checklist of “major mathematical problems.” The generative encounter model, on the other hand, conceptualizes mathematical progress as inherently open-ended and unfinished, and its development, for the time being, is subject to negotiation with definitions of human purpose, desire and experience.

“Mathematics is one of the greatest things humans have built. Like all our built things, it keeps changing as we change — and our understanding of it keeps changing too.”

The Checklist Model

Under the checklist model, mathematical progress consists of resolving well-defined, complex problems that are specified in advance. These include competition problems designed to measure the frontier of human mathematical capabilities such as those of the International Mathematical Olympiad, famous conjectures such as Fermat’s Last Theorem (or last conjecture), formalization benchmarks such as Freek Wiedijk’s list of 100 formalization challenges and prize problems such as Clay’s Millennium problems. Each of these can be considered an item on a checklist. Mathematical progress proceeds at rate at which the boxes get ticked, and reward and credit attribution goes to whoever ticks them first. This model of mathematical progress is attractive because it is neat and it makes progress easily measurable. That is why it underpins both the prestige economy of mathematics (Olympiad medals, the Fields Medal, the Millennium Prizes) and the benchmark culture of AI.

AI systems have been rapidly excelling at solving a checklist of major mathematical problems. Some mathematicians like Tao refer to a new age of “proof post-scarcity” in which checklists of mathematical conjectures, including ones to be added in the future, are quickly proved or disproved one after the other by increasingly powerful AI systems.

A subset of the mathematical community has long organized its conception of progress around this model and the straightforward systems for reward and credit that it produces. Whoever solves a major problem from a canonical checklist earns the credit, and that cements their status as a genius (often a lone genius, which is important). Entire research and academic institutions grew up around this incentive structure, and generations of students were taught that (one of) their highest aspirations should be to solve (at least) one of these problems. Now that AI systems can solve these problems, the norm that reserved such achievements exclusively for humans, and rewarded humans for them, no longer carries the social weight it once did. This means that, as Cornell mathematics professor Steven Strogatz said in a recent interview , the age of lone human mathematical heroes is over.

But the end of the lone human hero is not the end of human mathematicians.

AI is showing us that the incentives around the checklist model are not sustainable anymore. While loss and grief are valid responses to this new reality, remaining stuck there leaves the community unable to respond to radically transformative changes. We should look at this historical moment as an opportunity to redesign the structures that motivate and reward mathematical work, and we should do it soon.

“AI brings us back to an old philosophical question: Where does mathematics come from?”

The checklist model rests on a remarkably narrow conception of mathematical inquiry. Even before AI systems started solving problems, the model didn’t seem to directly serve real-world problems. Many mathematicians have long worked in “exploratory mode,” disregarding questions about whether their lines of inquiry had any practical usefulness. G.H. Hardy, an English mathematician who died in 1947, is famous for writing “I have never done anything ‘useful.’ No discovery of mine has made, or is likely to make, directly or indirectly, for good or ill, the least difference to the amenity of the world.”

If mathematical progress is bound to the values of human mathematicians who can decide what to formalize, determine which problems truly matter, co-create with software and artificial agents and invent or discover novel domains of inquiry, then AI does not signal an end for the field. Instead, it opens a vast, unprecedented space of possibility.

The checklist model of mathematical progress is not representative of the actual progress in “mathematics” when we look at the history of the field. Under its narrow view, the pessimism of some mathematicians ( We are becoming obsolete ; There is no need for future humans to do mathematics ; No valuable rewards for doing mathematics remain for humans now ) offers no guidance about what mathematicians should do next.

Under a different model of mathematical progress, which I call the generative encounter model, proving major problems is just one piece of “doing mathematics” or “being a mathematician.” Here, AI’s impact on the mathematical community, generational education and institutional design is much more open to constructive and creative adjustment.

The Generative Encounter Model

In 1939, George Dantzig arrived late to a statistics class during his doctoral studies at Berkeley and found two problems written on the blackboard. He thought they were homework assignments from the professor, Jerzy Neyman, so he solved them and handed in his work. “About six weeks later,” according to his own account, Dantzig and his wife “were awakened by someone banging on our front door. It was Neyman. He rushed in with papers in hand, all excited.” The problems weren’t homework, it turned out, but rather famous unsolved problems, and Neyman wanted to rush to publish Dantzig’s work.

After Berkeley, Dantzig became an adviser to the U.S. Air Force Comptroller. He was tasked with finding a way to mechanize the planning and budgeting of the military’s staggering logistical operations. The reality he faced was one of worldly complexity. Thousands of human clerks were tasked with drafting and creating supply-chain and personnel schedules entirely by hand, using heuristic trial-and-error.

There were no preexisting mathematical problems for Dantzig to solve here. He faced the chaotic physical reality and had to figure out how to translate it into a useful mathematical abstraction. This is an example of an “encounter” in the generative encounter model: a social and practical problem with apparently little to do with “just proving” mathematics.

As Dantzig himself later recounted in an interview, the military used the word “program” — not computer code but rather a plan or a schedule. Dantzig’s goal, therefore, became simply to more rapidly develop a program for time-staged deployment, training and logistics. He was not trying to prove a theorem or conjecture; he was not hired for that, nor did he expect an award for developing such a thing. He was trying to fix an administrative bottleneck.

To do so, he invented (or discovered, if you like) a class of problems that needed solving. He did this by structuring and interpreting the situation into an elegant formulation composed of two distinct parts: a linear objective to be achieved (maximize efficiency or minimize cost, for example) and a set of constraints expressed as a system of linear inequalities (a certain number of planes, pilots, gallons of fuel, etc.). He called this mathematical package a “linear programming problem.” The word “programming” he borrowed directly from the military’s administrative vocabulary.

By mathematically separating the physical constraints from the ultimate goal and approximating both with linear relationships, Dantzig mapped a messy real-world problem onto a clean, high-dimensional geometric object: a convex polyhedron. This abstraction transformed a question of scheduling human action and materials into a question of geometry, and in doing so, made it a part of an open-ended conception of mathematics .

Dantzig had taste. He made a crucial recognition: As a matter of mathematical necessity, the optimal solution to a programming problem would lie on one of the vertices of a polyhedron. The search for the “best” mathematical solution or the best “schedule” thus became a search for the “highest” corner of a geometric object. Dantzig then developed the now-famous simplex algorithm to systematically search for that optimal vertex by efficiently moving along the edges of the polyhedron until reaching the peak.

Before Dantzig, there was no mathematical community of “linear programmers” listing out problems in their field and seeking to solve them. He formed a community, one that grew to include operations researchers, mathematical economists and industrial engineers as additional sub-branches of the field were developed. This group defined itself by a shared interest in a set of problems that had not existed a decade earlier.

Linear programming works for continuous resources like gallons of fuel, but what if a problem demands whole units? You cannot fly half an airplane or assign a third of a pilot to a mission. That physical constraint, a new encounter, forced the invention of a branch of operations research known as integer programming . This, in turn, opened a vast new frontier of mathematics, generating entirely new branches of mathematics, theoretical models and novel algorithms, which themselves collided with new problems and produced yet more fields of inquiry .

“A revolution in automated proof discovery, on its own, guarantees nothing definite about the future of mathematics, which remains an open-ended domain of inquiry.”

Before the MIT mathematician Norbert Wiener created the field we now call cybernetics , which later formed the backbone of modern artificial intelligence, he was confronted with a wartime problem similar in some ways to the one that faced Dantzig: how to shoot a plane out of the sky using an antiaircraft gun on the ground when the enemy pilot was taking evasive action. Aiming at the plane guaranteed a miss, so where do you aim? As Wiener later put it, “It is exceedingly important to shoot the missile, not at the target, but in such a way that missile and target may come together in space at some time in the future. We must hence find some method of predicting the future position of the plane.” This problem was not on any checklist of mathematical problems. It had to be encountered.

Wiener’s move was to reframe the problem. He stopped treating a pilot as a strategic adversary to be outguessed and instead considered him a component in a system to be characterized. He saw that the pilot’s evasive maneuvers were not purely random; they were responses to the gunner’s actions and corrections against the aircraft’s physical lags. In this view, the gunner, the antiaircraft gun, the shell, the pilot and the aircraft all formed a single system with different feedback loops between them. To this loop Wiener added what he called a predictor.

In his 1948 book “ Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine ,” Wiener described the task as designing a predictor whose characteristics “depend[ed] on a long-time acquaintance with the statistics of the ensemble of time series which we desire to predict.” In this sentence, the significance of real-world encounters for mathematical progress becomes quite obvious. The physical problem of gunnery was converted into a statistical problem about time. This conversion created a cluster of new mathematical problems: What is the optimal filter to separate a signal from noise? How can one best predict the future course of a random process from its past? What, formally, does it even mean for a system to be goal-directed?

The answers gave birth to the theory of statistical filtering and prediction and ultimately the feedback formalism that organized the new mathematics and science of cybernetics. Wiener created a new branch of mathematics for describing, explaining, understanding and predicting control and communication in both machines and living organisms. It generated a new community, a new field, which brought different epistemic stances together to better understand the world. The now-famous Macy Conferences in the late 1940s and early 1950s brought together biologists, psychiatrists, anthropologists and engineers around a set of problems that previously had no disciplinary home. Cybernetics, as a new branch of mathematics, created a new home for such inquiries. Read Noema in print.

Most telling of all, the original purpose that sparked the work was soon superseded. Wiener’s antiaircraft predictor was not widely deployed; a simpler design from Bell Labs won the military contract. Had it been a problem on a checklist, Wiener’s project might be seen as a failure, seeing as how it was an inferior solution to another. But the mathematics it created survived and went on to reshape our understanding of many systems, from factory automation to human and artificial neural systems.

There Is No Distinction Between Pure And Applied Mathematics. There Is Only Mathematics.

During my doctoral studies in mathematics (in the field of “operations research”), I attended a national conference for mathematical graduate students in Canada. The atmosphere was charged with a peculiar intellectual stratification between “pure” (or “real”) mathematics and “applied” mathematics.

When some of my peers, who were working on classical analytic number theory and variations of the Riemann hypothesis, learned that others of us were researching mathematical and computational approaches for large-scale decision problems, their response was immediate and dismissive: What you do is not real mathematics. To them, real mathematical inquiry belonged exclusively to the solitary pursuit of proving major theorems within self-contained axiomatic systems. Not considered real mathematics were efforts to develop and formulate algorithms to solve large-scale decision problems, optimize resource distribution, translate frictions and decision problems into mathematical structures, and perhaps find new theories of decision-making in real-world encounters.

The culture of mathematicians has for generations harbored a hidden hierarchy between these two communities of mathematicians: Generating abstract proofs supposedly constituted “real” mathematics whereas dealing with the messy, empirical world was dismissed as an inferior craft. Historically, this divide served a practical purpose: It functioned as a tool for creating an epistemic division of labor, organizing mathematical activity and giving rise to separate institutions, journals and reward structures for tackling a variety of different cognitive engagements with mathematical problems.

By placing the generation of proofs for very complex problems at the apex of this hierarchy, the pure-applied dichotomy, perhaps unintentionally, popularized the idea that pure mathematics is (real) mathematics. In doing so, it enshrined the checklist model of mathematical progress, leading many to mistake measuring a peculiar type of epistemic activity for the entirety of mathematical progress. The conflation of the title mathematician with those who study only pure mathematics is a pervasive and uncritical cultural prejudice. It is one that relegates researchers who grapple with physical and systemic realities to second-class status. I think AI has forced us to correct that prejudice, and I do not think we can ignore it.

“A true golden age of mathematics, rooted in human purpose and new visions of education and collective reward, may have just begun.”

Dantzig too faced gatekeeping by pure mathematicians, whose insistence that their work was the only “real” mathematics generated a highly exclusionary perception of the discipline. When asked whether he thought of himself as an operations researcher or a mathematician, Dantzig answered: “I consider myself a mathematician. I don’t differentiate between pure mathematics and applied mathematics. I know other people will tell you there is a difference, but there isn’t.”

When the interviewer noted that pure mathematicians often describe operations researchers as “second-rate mathematicians playing with toy problems,” Dantzig’s response was characteristically blunt: “Mathematicians are snobs.”

“Present company excepted,” the interviewer responded. “Pure math involves clean problems, but real-world problems are messy.”

“Real-world problems are all dirty, that’s correct,” Dantzig said. “Any model of them is an approximation of reality; it’s not reality.”

Dantzig’s experience in the development of linear programming led him to become a strong advocate of encountered problems as the inspiration for interesting and challenging mathematical work. Speaking to Donald Albers in 1984, he said:

Just because my mathematics has its origin in a real problem doesn’t make it less interesting to me—just the other way around, I find it makes the puzzle I am working on all the more exciting. I get satisfaction out of knowing that I’m working on a relevant problem. I find that just as much mathematical ingenuity has to go into solving problems from a newly developing area as from some old so-called pure math area.

Operations research, Dantzig went on, is the “science of decision-making”: the art of “abstracting a problem and putting it into mathematical form.” For him, mathematical practice spans a continuous spectrum from the abstract theorist seeking formal solutions down to the practitioner needing an actionable answer to a concrete crisis. To chop this continuum in half and declare one end “noble” and the other “second-class” misses the entire dynamic essence of mathematical inquiry.

The “crisis” of AI’s ability to rapidly solve complex problems, and mathematicians’ responsibility for building infrastructure for mathematical inquiry in the near future, can be seen in a new light. A messy encounter with the world, after all, can be the birthplace of the purest mathematics, and pure mathematics can find its way back to the world.

Powerful Systems, Open Futures

We must approach this historical moment with the utmost care. The main challenge is not only to mourn a loss. It is, more importantly, to build a better future. The development and deployment of AI is forcing us to redraw the maps of human motivation, reward and research prestige in mathematics. Redrawing those maps does not have to erase human agency — but it can if approached clumsily.

If we restructure how we assign credit, set research priorities and reward work — moving away from proof discovery alone — we can cultivate “Dantzig-style” mathematical thinkers. These are people who use AI to free their creative faculties and push into deeper, more interesting or more urgent territory.

This moment has opened a vast space of possibilities. New incentives can be designed around problems that genuinely matter for better human life, for individual and social health, for planetary flourishing. And we are not short of those problems.

Perhaps the mathematical community and its future generations can move from “ Who proved it?” to “ Who decided this was worth proving, why, and how did we make sure it was right?” Large collaborations already exist in mathematics: the Polymath projects, the Lean community’s Mathlib, the long effort to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem. Mathematicians can coordinate around shared goals that matter for their community, but also for the world.

They now need to scale coordination capabilities. But how?

I think the mathematical community must embrace the generative encounter model of mathematical progress. This requires that we treat the integration of AI in mathematics as a rich, independent subject of foundational analysis. Far from signaling the end of mathematics, this opens room for examining a vast frontier of urgent, encountered mathematical problems that require deep work, often in collaboration with other disciplines. Here are four critical clusters of mathematical problems where this work is urgently needed:

Provably safe cyber infrastructure . Our global digital systems remain profoundly fragile. Human mathematicians, using AI as a high-throughput collaborative partner, can work to find the flaws and rebuild our cyber foundations from first principles, establishing provably secure and mathematically verified computing environments.

The epistemic mechanics of deep learning . Our mathematical grasp of how neural networks learn, generalize and represent high-dimensional data is still in its infancy. Several concerns about advanced AI causing catastrophic harm originate directly from this gap in understanding. Despite significant advances, developing a rigorous “mathematical science of deep learning” remains a fundamental challenge, and solving it is a precondition for building truly trustworthy systems.

The mathematics of multi-agent control . The dynamic alignment or misalignment of interacting, agentic AI systems remains poorly understood . We need to draw on mathematical disciplines such as mathematical security, safety engineering, robust mechanism design and game theory to analyze how individually optimized agents behave when they coordinate, compete or collide.

The epistemology of machine-generated proofs . What should we do with AI-generated “proofs” that are too long, too complex, or too alien for human minds to understand or verify ? Rather than rejecting them because they are unintelligible, we must develop new mathematical techniques for explanation, logical translation and interactive verification that make them understandable. We shouldn’t rush to rely on such proofs, but these techniques can give us reliable paths for turning raw automated output into genuine human understanding.

None of these problems appear on a checklist of mathematical problems. None of them will be easily “solved” by a single human mathematician. Each needs teams of humans equipped with technological tools to decide what and how to formalize and interpret mathematical problems that matter — and how to build institutions to apply the offered solutions.

The world around us is human-made: the buildings, the networks, the institutions, the AI models themselves. Mathematics is one of the greatest things humans have built. Like all our built things, it keeps changing as we change — and our understanding of it keeps changing too.

This brings us back to an old philosophical question: Where does mathematics come from? The cognitive scientists George Lakoff and Rafael Núñez gave one answer in their book “ Where Mathematics Comes From ”: embodied human cognition. Platonists give another: Mathematics is discovered, not made. Its objects exist independently of humans, and mathematicians are explorers of a terrain that has been there all along and will still be there in the absence of any human. Formalists give a third response: Mathematics is a game of symbols and rules, and it is “true” only in the sense that a legal chess move is correct. I won’t settle the debate here. But every answer locates at least part of the origin of mathematics in an encounter: between minds and the world, between us and Plato’s heaven, or between human communities and the questions they find worth asking and answering. AI systems have now become a serious participant in that encounter.

A revolution in automated proof discovery, on its own, guarantees nothing definite about the future of mathematics, which remains an open-ended domain of inquiry. That future will be shaped not only by AIs but also by the preconditions that make doing mathematics possible, or impossible: the purposes, infrastructure and institutions we build around the questions we find worth asking and answering. These include how to verify results, how to assign credit, how to train students, how to value human cognition and agency, how to support those harmed by this transition and give them new systems of recognition to rely on, how to advance human and planetary flourishing, how to make tools and infrastructure broadly accessible and who sits at the table when these questions are answered.

Answering these questions requires science and mathematics as necessary elements of the sociotechnical foundation for a better future. And that we do not yet have.

“New incentives can be designed around problems that genuinely matter for better human life, for individual and social health, for planetary flourishing. And we are not short of those problems.”

Viewed from the generative encounter model of mathematical progress, a true golden age of mathematics, rooted in human purpose and new visions of education and collective reward, may have just begun.

Suppose this situation and these questions are only temporary. What about later? What if we eventually build artificial superintelligence — systems that don’t just prove theorems but pose questions, judge which ones matter, design curricula and decide how rewards are distributed? Systems that automate the whole process of generative encounters?

The deepest version of the worry some “pure” mathematicians are articulating is not whether AI can automate mathematical proofs. It is whether AI eventually automates human purpose itself. But let’s not forget how we arrived here.

Our current moment is, among other things, a long-term consequence of the dream of formalizing mathematics, from the well-posed formulas of mathematical logic that gave rise to software engineering to the contemporary drive in the Lean community to formalize mathematics in machine-readable form so that machines might verify and, one day, prove or solve problems. In some sense, where we are today is partly the realization of a long dream held by a portion of the mathematical community. But living in a realized dream requires us to think carefully not just about the dream itself, but about its consequences. Purpose matters.

Whether the day ever comes when human purpose is fully automated none of us can know. But what is clear is that the future is shaped by what we dream and build today, and we owe it to ourselves, our children and future generations to dream and build it with care. In the end, the transition to the future is not separate from the future. And the transition is where the future is actually lived, dreamed and made.

Author’s note: Thanks to Jim Brown, Marcus Hutter and Shane Legg for comments on this essay.

stories.title: Free the Kremlin’s Political Prisoners—and Stop Sending It New Ones
stories.summary: The Trump administration’s one-off deals won’t empty Russia’s prisons—especially while U.S. deportations are refilling them. The post Free the Kremlin’s Political Prisoners—and Stop Sending It New Ones appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shutterstock

In late September, The Atlantic reported that U.S. President Donald Trump had greenlit plans to offer Russia sanctions relief in exchange for the release of political prisoners.

With peace talks still deadlocked after more than a year of U.S. diplomacy, sanctions remain a vital check on Russia’s ability to wage war against Ukraine. In the following weeks, however, Trump struck a diesel deal with Vladimir Putin and waived new sanctions on Russian oil and gas. This provoked backlash from Kyiv, but Trump insisted that he was making “great progress” with Russia, including on “hostage negotiations.”

Then, on October 21, the Kremlin freed Stephen Hubbard , a 74-year-old American citizen held in Russian captivity for over four years. In statements about the release , Trump said that the United States “was not required to give anything in return,” while admitting that enforcing tougher sanctions would have halted negotiations for Hubbard’s freedom.

As critics note, the release of Hubbard cost Putin little, and making concessions risks incentivizing the regime to take more hostages. At the same time, a glaring contradiction is being overlooked. While Washington negotiates to free some prisoners, its immigration policy is funneling new ones into Russia’s jails.

Who the Kremlin Holds

No one knows exactly how many people Russia has arbitrarily detained in connection with its war against Ukraine. The international human rights campaign People First! estimates tens of thousands; most are Ukrainian civilians imprisoned across Russia and occupied Ukraine. These “ghost prisoners” are held without formal charges. They are tortured and kept incommunicado, with no access to lawyers, relatives, or international organizations.

In occupied Crimea, where Russia has enforced one of its harshest regimes since 2014, Ukrainian authorities have identified 223 political prisoners, including 155 Crimean Tatars and many with serious health problems .

According to OVD-Info data , at least 2,368 people are currently imprisoned in Russia for political reasons. The number of politically motivated criminal proceedings is even higher, with more than 5,000 active cases.

The #free120 campaign puts the total number of critically ill political prisoners at 406. Every year, several die behind bars.

People First! calls for any negotiated peace agreement to prioritize the immediate release of all these captives, alongside the return of Ukrainian children forcibly taken to Russia, the repatriation of POWs held by both sides, and the release of Belarusians imprisoned for their anti-war views.

When it comes to hostage negotiations, which are often treated as a separate diplomatic track, priority should go to the most vulnerable: minors and the elderly, the seriously ill, torture victims, and those targeted for their sexuality, ethnicity, or faith. One-off exchanges offer no transparent or permanent mechanism for deciding who goes free.

In talks with Russia, Washington has long focused on freeing specific individuals, particularly its own citizens. In December 2022, for example, the Biden administration agreed to a controversial one-for-one exchange, trading notorious Russian arms dealer Victor Bout for Brittney Griner, an American basketball star imprisoned in Russia on drug charges.

Two years later, the United States orchestrated the biggest prisoner swap between Russia and Western countries since the Cold War. The Kremlin ultimately handed over 16 people—most of them Russian political prisoners—in exchange for eight FSB agents, hackers, and spies.

These releases were humanitarian achievements: unjustly imprisoned people regained their freedom, and lives were likely saved—even if the Russians among them were forced into exile . However, releases alone do not change what puts people behind bars. So long as the laws used to punish dissent remain in force, new cases will keep coming.

The John Coale Approach—and an Alternative

The Kremlin has denied holding any political prisoners or engaging in talks on sanctions relief with American officials. But Trump’s nomination of John Coale as U.S. envoy for hostage affairs suggests plans to replicate his strategy as special envoy to Belarus.

Having built a rapport with authoritarian leader Aleksander Lukashenko, Coale has secured the release of more than 500 political prisoners in exchange for easing U.S. sanctions. However, this has turned repression into a revolving door, with Minsk freeing certain people while continuing to imprison others on political grounds.

During Coale’s last meeting with Lukashenko in September, the United States hoped to free 200 more political prisoners. He came away with 25 people in return for lifting U.S. sanctions on two Belarusian companies. According to Viasna, a leading Belarusian human rights group, at least 10 others were prepared for release and then sent back to their cells, likely due to the outcome of the talks.

At least 88 5 political prisoners remain behind bars in Belarus today. Every one is a person with loved ones awaiting their release; under current U.S. policy, each is also a potential bargaining chip.

If the Senate confirms Coale’s new position, his portfolio will expand to include Russia, among other authoritarian countries. Negotiations with such regimes demand a consistent strategy to save lives and effect systemic change.

To this end, Washington should push for the following simultaneously:

the immediate release of Ukrainian civilians and political prisoners held by Russia;

the repeal of repressive legislation targeting freedom of speech and civil society organizations (such as the laws on military censorship, “foreign agents,” and “undesirable” organizations);

an end to the arbitrary use of anti-terrorism, anti-extremism, and national-security laws, including those on treason and espionage frequently used to target and severely punish political opponents and Ukrainian citizens.

At the very least, the United States should demand that the Kremlin disclose the identities and whereabouts of all detainees, and provide international organizations full access to them.

Handing the Kremlin New Hostages

Unfortunately, Washington is helping refill the Kremlin’s “hostage bank.” Under the Trump administration’s deportation policy, Russians facing political persecution are being denied asylum in the United States and returned to their home country.

According to the BBC , removals surpassed 1,200 in 2025, up from 222 in 2023. Among these deportees were anti-war dissidents and army deserters, some of whom were handed military summonses, sent to the front, or arrested upon their return to Russia.

The imprisonment of activist Leonid Melekhin is a case in point. Melekhin spent 10 months in U.S. immigration detention, only to have his asylum bid rejected in July 2025. He was then deported to Russia, where he was arrested upon arrival on “terrorism” charges. On October 5, a Russian court sentenced Melekhin to six years in prison.

The activist’s time in U.S. detention reportedly “broke him” (Melekhin’s state-appointed lawyer in Russia claims that he “asked to be sent back” to Russia). The conditions in ICE detention facilities are indeed concerning. As of this writing, Russian asylum seekers in at least three detention centers have joined hunger strikes to protest alleged mistreatment and poor conditions.

The Trump administration can act preemptively to support those facing political persecution in their home country. It should halt deportations, guarantee fair asylum hearings, end prolonged detentions, and protect dissidents, journalists, and those who refuse to fight.

Freeing political prisoners is among diplomacy’s most humane goals. To have the greatest impact, Washington should pair negotiations for releases with sustained pressure to dismantle the laws that fill prisons—and ensure that those who escape persecution find refuge, not a return ticket to a cell.

stories.summary: A Surrey coroner raises concerns over HM Treasury procedures following the death of Chloe Moffat.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
HM Treasury says it accepts a coroner's concerns after Chloe Moffat, the PA to one of its directors, took her own life

Published 30 October 2026, 17:05 GMT

The Treasury has accepted it contributed to the death of a personal assistant and said "immediate steps" have been taken to tackle outstanding risks.

Chloe Moffat, 26, took her own life in May 2025, the day after managers told her of allegations that she had shared sensitive confidential information, which she denied.

A coroner found a practice within HM Treasury of "informal fact-finding" meetings with employees accused of misconduct had no basis in the ministry's policy and posed a risk of future death.

Responding, the Treasury and the Cabinet Office wrote that they "accept the concerns identified" and "take them extremely seriously".

The Cabinet Office said it would also undertake a wider review of workplace conflict and resolution across Whitehall within a year.

At Moffat's inquest in August, the Treasury was found to have "materially contributed" to her death by not telling her that the likely penalty if allegations against her were proven would be a written warning and not dismissal.

In a response to the coroner's report , external , the Treasury "accepted the findings in the report in full" and said it had taken immediate action to mitigate the concerns raised.

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line

Strengthened "wellbeing safeguards" had been introduced and the use of informal fact-finding meetings had been stopped while a full policy review was conducted, the department said.

Employees facing misconduct allegations would be informed of the possible outcomes before being asked to respond and a suicide prevention framework was being developed, it added.

"HM Treasury has considered these concerns carefully and has taken immediate steps to mitigate the identified risks," according to the department's response.

"While this work introduces some enhancements, much of it is intended to strengthen, clarify and build on the procedures and support already in place."

A Treasury spokesperson added: "The Treasury's deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe's friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague.

"An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout."

stories.title: Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree
stories.summary: The new government office in Manchester has launched 50 job adverts for roles including a "rewiring the state deputy director".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham made opening No10 North one of his first acts as PM

Published 4 hours ago

Andy Burnham's Number 10 North has gone on a multi-million pound hiring spree with dozens of new jobs being advertised.

The office in Manchester, set up by the prime minister in July, has launched 50 external job adverts, including a "rewiring the state deputy director".

It is the latest sign of how pivotal the government outpost - designed as a sister office to London's Downing Street - may prove to Burnham's aim to devolve power across the country.

Government sources say the roles will be paid for out of existing budgets.

The new recruits "will work with mayors and councils to identify barriers holding places back", but the Conservatives have described the office as a "gimmick".

There will be no redundancies elsewehere in the civil service as a result of the hiring spree, the BBC has been told, with some jobs expected to be relocated and other vacant roles closed.

The new roles, all based in Manchester, cover areas including strategy, communications, engagement, private office and policy.

BBC News has calculated they total up to £2.8m for basic salaries alone, excluding employer pension contributions in the civil service of 28.97%.

No10 North now has 120 members of staff, nearly half of the 280 staff who work in No10 London.

Among the highest paid of the roles are a "rewiring the state deputy director", with a salary band of £86,000 to £117,000, who will "lead the Rewiring the State Unit... shaping the government's approach to devolution across departments".

The government said it was launching a recruitment campaign for staff who would "bring fresh perspectives and knowledge of the places they serve, moving decisions closer to the people they affect".

No10 North "is driving the most significant transfer of power out of Westminster in a generation," the government added in a statement.

No10 North is designed as a sister office to London's Downing Street - with a replica black door inside on show

Some apprenticeships and secondments are also being advertised.

It comes as the government confirmed on Friday that No10 North would move from its current temporary home in Heron House, on Manchester's Albert Square, to a new government office on First Street in spring 2027.

No10 North will share the city centre building with other government departments spanning business, education, local government and the Cabinet Office.

Burnham made opening No10 North one of his first acts as prime minister , describing it as "the nerve-centre of a rewired Britain" that would help bring growth to more areas of Britain.

No10 North's deputy director Duncan Parish said in a speech last week that officials faced "institutional challenges" with delivering on these aims and called for a "mindset shift" across the UK's central government.

Conservative Party deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "He [Burnham] promised to streamline the civil service, but now he is hiring extra staff and, once again, won't say where the money is coming from.

"Manchesterism is just more bureaucracy at taxpayers' expense."

Meanwhile, Tory shadow cabinet minister Mike Wood has said there is "so little transparency" around No10 North after ministers told him they could not reveal figures on headcounts and office attendance.

According to the new job adverts, the Office for the Prime Minister - with exceptions for certain roles - expects No10 staff to be in the office a minimum of 60% of the time.

Since opening, No10 North has hosted summits of regional mayors, at least two of which have been partly held as video calls on Microsoft Teams. At one of these meetings, ministers unveiled controversial powers for mayors in England to charge new fees on visitors' overnight stays.

It has also hosted an education summit of school leaders and Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin met Burnham for the first time as PM at No10 North in September.

stories.body:
Andy Burnham and Rhun ap Iorwerth met in Glasgow on Friday

Published 30 October 2026, 07:17 GMT

Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth says there has been a "significant step forward" with regards to his country's spending and borrowing powers after meeting the prime minister.

Andy Burnham held a meeting of his National Economic Council with the first ministers of Wales and Scotland on Friday, after which ap Iorwerth said it was a matter of "how and when" a loosening of financial restrictions will take place.

At the summit in Glasgow, Burnham lobbied the government leaders to devolve "deeper" to the regions of Wales and Scotland.

The prime minister said the two first ministers had agreed to work with him on "regional empowerment".

No timescales were announced for changes to Wales' finances.

Friday's meeting followed rows between the Welsh and UK government over the chancellor's Budget on Wednesday, which ap Iorwerth had said was "not serious about Wales".

His party Plaid Cymru said the budget left the Welsh government with a real-terms cut in funding, which the UK government denied.

Rhun ap Iorwerth, John Swinney, joined by Welsh Finance Minister Elin Jones, attended the meeting on Friday

Ap Iorwerth had set out a range of demands to the prime minister in a letter sent at the start of October.

As well as calling for powers over policing and justice, and for more funding for rail projects, he called for an end to restrictions on access to the Wales reserve - spare funding that the Welsh government can store in one year to use in another.

It is capped at £385m, and the Welsh government can only draw down £137.5m and £55m for resource and capital spend respectively per year.

The Welsh government can also borrow up to £1.1bn for infrastructure, with a limit of £165m a year.

Ap Iorwerth said: "There were some real positives here.

"On fiscal flexibility, the ability for us to use our funding better in Wales, use our reserves better in Wales - and on borrowing powers, I was told clearly that its now was a matter of how and when. That is a significant step forward."

He said there was "clearly an interest" for the prime minister to "really understand that sheer injustice of underfunding of rail in Wales that we have seen for many years".

"That is a particular issue we will be taking forward now between my office and his," he said.

On policing, the first minister said "I think instinctively the prime minister wants to go there and there's still work to do".

At a speech this month the first minister called for "practical agreement" on how the two governments could work together on the economy, calling for Westminster to avoid duplication in areas that are devolved already to the Welsh government.

Burnham said Friday's meeting was "positive", and that both first ministers had agreed to "work together jointly on regional empowerment in Scotland and Wales as well".

"We now have a process where we have detailed work by officials on both sides to see if we can come to a set of arrangements that are right for Scotland and right for Wales," Burnham said.

"We had a good discussion today on two fronts, one around re-industrialisation and the offer of more devolution of innovation funding to the regional level."

He said it was for Scotland and Wales to decide how that looks.

Burnham also said the UK government will now look at arrangements for further devolution of employment support.

Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock fiscal flexibilities and borrowing was on the agenda for future Welsh government discussions with No 10 North.

"It is going to take some conversations on how that would work in practice.

"I can't give you a specific time frame as things stand," he said.

Following Wednesday's Budget, which saw an extra £450m announced for Wales over the next three years as well as funding for individual projects, the Welsh government claimed the extra money would represent a real-terms cut to its own finances.

A £30m funding pledge for a new railway station in Cardiff was also described as "an insult" by Wales' transport minister.

On Radio Wales Breakfast on Friday before the summit, ap Iorwerth said there were "paltry sums of money coming on rail, when they've said there's £14bn on the way" and a "real terms cut in the money we have to spend on public services".

"The Budget was not serious about Wales," he said.

He said in another interview he could "only assume that the prime minister is holding something back".

Ap Iorwerth told BBC Wales that Wednesday's Budget had "so little mention" of his nation

After the meeting, Downing Street said ap Iorwerth had "agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode".

"This would be a policy sprint led by No 10 North, involving officials from each government, to take this agenda forward," they said.

Ap Iorwerth said in a statement: "There was an encouraging consensus that the fiscal and borrowing powers which have for so long put Wales at a disadvantage compared with other UK nations must be revised as a matter of urgency.

"I welcome the prime minister's comments that this is now a matter of how and when."

Welsh ministers had called for changes to their borrowing rules and assurances that child poverty payments it wants to introduce would leave recipients' tax and benefits allowances unaffected.

None of that was addressed in the Budget, although Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock has said "positive" talks were continuing regarding the child poverty payments.

Friday's meeting of the National Economic Council - a summit to help boost the UK economy - was due to be attended by the prime minister and all the devolved leaders.

However, it emerged on Thursday that Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill would not be there after her attendance was blocked by her Democratic Unionist Party (DUP).

Since he became prime minister, Burnham has consistently spoken in favour of devolution.

He has said he is "open" to transferring powers over policing and justice to Wales and, during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, he said he was "ready to make an offer" on the devolution of employment support.

Jensen Huang reported to have had close relationship with tech company executive suspected of passing intel to China

US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by an alleged Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.

Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China , prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.

In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.

White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he has developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.

The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.

In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.

stories.title: Winter fuel cuts turned the Welsh against Labour, former leader Neil Kinnock says
stories.summary: The former Labour leader says welfare policies turned disillusionment with Labour into "active dislike".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Lord Kinnock says UK Labour decisions led to "dislike" of the Welsh arm of the party

Published 7 hours ago

Former Labour leader Neil Kinnock says the party's welfare policies turned disillusionment with Labour in Wales into "active dislike".

He said that UK government decisions on benefits and winter fuel payments had driven voters in Wales away from the Welsh arm of the party before the country's Senedd election in May.

Lord Kinnock made the comments as part of a Newyddion S4C , external YouTube special on Andy Burnham's first 100 days as prime minister.

Governing "at both ends of the M4" before Wales' parliamentary elections had presented an extra challenge for his party, he said.

Winter fuel payments fell by 9.3 million before U-turn Published 16 September 2025

He said: "If there is any opposition or resentment to the government on either end of the M4, the other lot are going to pay as well.

"There is no doubt in my mind," he said, that "alienation... had been creeping up".

"It could be a mixture of boredom. It could be a mixture of dislike," Kinnock said.

He said "what turned that into active dislike" had been things "like the withdrawal of the winter fuel allowance, the threats to the welfare system" and not scrapping a cap on two child benefits quick enough.

In June last year, the Labour UK government U-turned on its controversial decision to means-test winter fuel payments for pensioners in England and Wales.

Almost one year later, Labour lost power in Wales in a seismic election in May , returning just nine Senedd members after running the Welsh government for 27 years.

Lord Kinnock, who is the father of Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock , also said he had reservations about devolving justice to Wales - a key demand of the Plaid Cymru Welsh government.

Plaid ministers say it would allow for a more effective system tailored to Welsh communities and better integrated with health, housing and education.

Kinnock said there would no be "much of an argument" against the idea if it meant that "Wales was better protected, that the streets were safer" and "that the justice system was more efficient".

"But those guarantees are absent at the moment," he said.

"Until they exist, until they're in place, the upheaval of creating what would have to be effectively a new system with new management... with an introverted view of the justice system - there would be more downsides than upsides.

"Now that picture might change, but as I can see it now in October 2026, that's where we are, there are more disadvantages than advantages."

stories.summary: Drew Creek joins the Labour party after the policy motion was passed earlier this month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Newquay Mayor Drew Creek said he could not stand by the Greens' Zionism is racism motion

Published 7 hours ago

The leader of the Green Party on Cornwall Council has defected following the party's recent "Zionism is racism" motion.

Drew Creek joined the Labour and Co-operatives on Thursday after the policy motion was passed at the Green Party's conference earlier this month.

Creek, who is Mayor of Newquay and serves as a councillor for Trenance ward, said he had "huge respect" for Greens across Cornwall but the motion "crossed a line".

The Cornwall Green Party said it was "deeply saddened" by Creek's decision to join Labour and said it does not "try to impose uniformity of belief" among its members and elected representatives.

More news stories for Cornwall

Listen to the latest news for Cornwall

The motion backed by Green members at its party conference said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It has been criticised by Jewish groups , as well as some Green MPs and opposition political parties .

Creek said he hoped the Green Party would step back from the stance – but said instead, "Zack Polanski and the leadership has doubled down".

"I can't stand behind that, and I won't pretend otherwise," the councillor said.

He added: "People in Newquay don't want politicians driving division. They want someone who'll fix the roads, protect our coast, fight for local services and bring people together.

"That's the kind of politics I believe in and the kind of politics Andy Burnham has shown.

Zack Polanski previously said he would not overturn the motion

"Newquay is my home and where I am raising my family. I came into politics for one reason, to stand up for this town and the people in it. Labour is where I believe I can do that best, and I'm looking forward to getting on with the job."

Councillor Kate Ewert, Labour and Co-operative Group Leader on Cornwall Council said Creek's decision "highlights the serious questions about Zack Polanski's leadership".

Noah Law, MP for St Austell and Newquay, added: "In this period of polarised politics, it takes great courage to stand up for what you believe in.

"Having worked with Drew since my election, I have always found him to be steadfast in his beliefs, easy to work with, and a good advocate for Newquay."

'Disagreements'

A spokesperson for the Cornwall Green Party said Creek had "done excellent work as a Green councillor" and they understood there were "different views within the Green Party on the 'Zionism is Racism' motion".

They said: "Disagreements over the wording of this one motion should not distract from the fact that the Green Party is united in its condemnation of the racist genocide and ethnic cleansing that Israel is perpetrating in Gaza and the occupied territories, and united in its demand for much tougher sanctions on Israel.

"Labour, by contrast, refuses even to recognise that what we are seeing is genocide, and continues to allow arms exports to and intelligence-sharing with the government that is committing it.

"It's hard to see how anyone who is serious about action on climate, action to end extreme inequality, and action to prevent an ongoing genocide could switch their support to a party that is not serious about any of these."

stories.title: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
stories.summary: The government is under pressure to set out a path to greater defence spending, as ministers unveil plans to boost UK firms.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Wes Streeting has defended the government's current approach

Published 30 October 2026, 08:27 GMT

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.

The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.

It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.

Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.

The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.

Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.

While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.

Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather than announced in the Budget .

He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".

Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".

Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.

"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."

He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments to cut their capital budgets by 1% .

Labour MP Tan Dhesi has led the latest criticism of government defence spending

Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.

"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."

Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".

He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".

He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".

"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.

Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and the Nato-wide target of 3.5% by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.

Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".

Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.

In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.

But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".

"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.

stories.title: Mayors will be free to use share of tax to give residents grants
stories.summary: The Tory Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen says he's working on what he's calling a "tax rebate scheme".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
English mayors - such as those pictured here - are getting more control over funding

Published 8 hours ago

English regional mayors due to be handed a share of tax revenues by central government will be free to use it to give cash grants to individual residents and businesses, it has emerged.

In his Budget, Chancellor John Healey unveiled plans to allow mayors to keep some cash from income tax and business rates collected locally, describing it as "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants local leaders to be given more control over how money is spent in their areas to boost economic growth and services.

But Conservative Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen says he has been given assurances that he will be able to give grants to local residents instead.

Lord Houchen told the BBC he is working on a voluntary scheme that would give local residents the opportunity to apply for a share of the tax distributed to his region.

He said Treasury officials had told him this would be acceptable within the government's rules around the devolution of funding.

"It's a technical point around spending decisions," Lord Houchen told the BBC.

He said devolution of funding was a "good thing" and "means mayors are able to decide spending commitments, which includes rebates".

The BBC has been told mayors could choose to use the tax revenues they received from the government to offer grants to individual residents or businesses.

But any mayor who decided to use the money in this way would have less for other local priorities, such as housing and transport.

Lord Houchen has described his proposal as a "tax rebate scheme".

The Treasury would regard these payments as grants, because His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) is the only government authority in the UK that can issue income tax rebates.

Most of England's 14 strategic authorities are led by Labour mayors who have welcomed the move to give them a portion of income tax receipts.

Sources close to Reform UK's Greater Lincolnshire Mayor Andrea Jenkyns, and her counterpart in Hull and East Yorkshire, Luke Campbell, say they are waiting for more details to fully understand how they could use these tax revenues to benefit their regions.

Conservative Tees Valley Mayor Lord Houchen says fiscal devolution is a "good thing"

The government published its broad approach , external to reforming funding for local and regional government in England after Wednesday's Budget.

As it stands, mayors of English strategic authorities receive most of their funding from ring-fenced grants, allocated by central government to be spent on specific policy areas.

From April 2028, all mayors of strategic authorities in England will be assigned a share of basic-rate income tax generated in their areas.

Each mayor will receive a bespoke funding allocation that takes into account regional inequalities in tax bases, with the exact amounts to be set at the government's spending review next year.

"The government is not devolving the power to set income tax rates or thresholds to mayors but will be granting significantly more flexibility as to how assigned revenues are spent locally," the government's plan says.

"Mayors will be able to choose where to target funding, for example whether to maintain funding for local transport or prioritise other interventions."

From next year, mayors will also receive a 20% share of locally retained business rates.

This will be the first step towards allowing local and mayoral authorities to retain 100% of their business rates income before the end of the decade.

From 2028, strategic authorities led by mayors will also be given the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy, often dubbed a "tourist tax".

This charge will be an uncapped levy as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.

Labour mayors in 10 city regions said they would voluntarily limit the charge to 5% , but others - such as Lord Houchen - said they would not introduce the levy.

Burnham - who used to be a mayor himself in Greater Manchester - argues that funding and decision-making powers are too centralised in the UK.

The share of national taxes collected at a local level in the UK is 5.8%, the lowest in the G7, according to the OECD , external , a global policy forum.

That share is far below that of other countries with large economies such as France (20.4%), Japan (36%) and the US (45.7%).

But critics of fiscal devolution raise concerns about local capability, and inequalities between areas.

The Centre for Cities think tank says some areas may not have the expertise to manage developed powers effectively, risking deeper economic inequalities between areas.

The think tank supports fiscal devolution and believes it can offer significant benefits, if the challenges are managed effectively.

The Tees Valley Combined Authority (TVCA) led by Lord Houchen is facing a government inspection into its finances, after Local Government Minister Jim McMahon said he had concerns about its "long-term financial sustainability".

The authority said it welcomed the scrutiny and would continue to make improvements where needed.

Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loom

The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.

Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.

Estimates ranged from ⁠a 1% growth rate to a 4.2% pace.

The growth comes as resilient consumer spending and AI -driven ⁠business investment has more than ⁠offset the impact ​of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East .

The change is in stark contrast to ​households’ downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in ‌ Donald Trump ’s record-low approval ratings ‌and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment.

The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of about 2%. New data from the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, showed that prices increased 0.5% for the month in September and the annualized inflation rate rose to 3.6%. In August, the PCE’s inflation rate was 3.4%.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to an annualized 3.1%.

The consumer price index , a separate measure of inflation released by the Department of Labor that was released earlier in October, had also shown inflation rising in September, with the annualized inflation rate going from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September.

Despite the rise in prices, the US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4% range while acknowledging that inflation “remains elevated”.

Increasing interest rates can slow inflation, at the risk of slackening economic activity and the jobs market. Because inflation is still hot, economists expect the Fed to raise rates in December. The Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh, told reporters “economic activity is expanding ‌at a strong pace,” noting that “while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.”

Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the ​strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects, in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect ⁠this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.

Consumer spending, ​which accounts for more ​than two-thirds of the economy, increased at ​a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in ​the second quarter. Historically low ‌layoffs and moderate ​hiring are helping ​to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged behind inflation.

But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon – about $1 a gallon more than a year ago – as the US-Israel war on Iran drags on, economists anticipate a slowdown in consumer spending.

Multiple polls have shown Donald Trump’s approval rating on the economy have plummeted in the weeks before the election, with voters citing frustration over rising gas and grocery prices. Overall consumer sentiment , measured by the University of Michigan is down 15% from February, before the start of the war with Iran, as consumers expect more inflation to come.

Thinktank says chancellor has given himself a mountain to climb after ducking big decisions in low-key speech

John Healey has paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year after his budget failed to cover a £28bn shortfall in the public finances needed to avoid a return to austerity, according to Britain’s leading tax and spending experts.

A day after his address to the Commons , the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the chancellor had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking several big decisions in his debut tax and spending statement.

After his low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, the thinktank said Healey had left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms.

But as the war in the Middle East fuels a surge in inflation – raising the cost of delivering public services – the chancellor has in effect pencilled in large cuts in the run-up to the next general election.

Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.

“It effectively implies that some public services will see real-terms cuts in next year’s spending review,” she said.

With Labour having promised there would be no return to austerity, and as Andy Burnham’s government prepares for the next election, she said it appeared extremely unlikely that Healey would follow through with such cuts.

“A clear short-term risk with the chancellor’s choices is that next year – with low headroom and a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments – we see another season of damaging speculation about tax rises,” she said.

In his first budget as chancellor on Wednesday, Healey raised taxes on banks and landlords to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock emanating from the Middle East war.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – allowing a hit to the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drives up the UK government’s borrowing costs.

after newsletter promotion

Faced with grim forecasts for household living standards and growth in the British economy, the IFS said it was a “reasonable choice” for the chancellor to allow for a modest reduction in headroom.

However, his deferral of some important decisions to next year’s spending review prompted the thinktank to criticise his plans for meeting the fiscal rules, because they in effect relied on him cutting public spending or announcing tax increases that he had yet to prepare the public for.

“My concern is not that it would be impossible to deliver the implied cuts to other services – that could be done. But I’m sceptical that this government would be willing to do it,” Miller said.
